title: Most People Can't Read This Newsletter
subtitle: Literacy is also a huge issue, when limited, for our health.
body_html:
Reading and writing haven’t been a universal ability throughout human history:

Literacy rates in Western European countries during the Middle Ages were below twenty percent of the population. For most countries, literacy rates did not experience significant increases until the Enlightenment and industrialization.

The ability to read, by most people, has also been a key to unlocking a better future:

Two early exceptions to this broad trend were the Netherlands and England, which had achieved literacy rates above fifty percent of their populations by the mid-seventeenth century.

Being able to read allowed the Brits and Dutch, and thus their colonies, like the Americans, to take advantage of reading and writing to accelerate their economic growth. And these two cohorts also aggressively pursued the “venture capital” high-risk/high-reward activities of the day more than any other cultures at the time. Yes, that is overwhelmingly whaling. There is a remarkable 3-part series on the topic done by Freakonomics—strongly recommended.

I'm trying to think through whether reading still matters, and writing, as someone who is a writer, which relies on other people who can read to engage with the work that I'm doing.

Now we have other ways to communicate; it's not just writing anymore. You can make videos. They can be as short as just a couple of seconds. I actually do some of that to get the word out to people who are not readers.

But what degree does the fall of writing and reading presage the fall of everything we hold dear?

Not being able to read isn’t just bad for the readership of a newsletter. That is—of course—the most relevant thing to myself as a John-Galt-capitalist; however, it also has health effects that are deleterious. Sorry, “that are bad:”

Patients with low literacy had poorer health outcomes, including knowledge, intermediate disease markers, measures of morbidity, general health status, and use of health resources. Patients with low literacy were generally 1.5 to 3 times more likely to experience a given poor outcome.1

It’s hard to be health literate when you can’t read any words, much less health-related words, and low health literacy itself has devastating consequences:

Low health literacy was consistently associated with more hospitalizations; greater use of emergency care; lower receipt of mammography screening and influenza vaccine; poorer ability to demonstrate taking medications appropriately; poorer ability to interpret labels and health messages; and, among elderly persons, poorer overall health status and higher mortality rates. Poor health literacy partially explains racial disparities in some outcomes.2

It’s detrimental for young people, but it worsens as we age. It may explain some portions of racial disparities. It’s a big problem.

Low literacy is associated (in an old study) with increased risk of hospitalizations:

Patients with inadequate literacy were twice as likely as patients with adequate literacy to be hospitalized during 1994 and 1995 (31.5% vs 14.9%, p < .001). After adjusting for age, gender, race, self-reported health, socioeconomic status, and health insurance, patients with inadequate literacy were more likely to be hospitalized than patients with adequate literacy (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.69; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.13, 2.53).

And in those with prior admissions, it was ever worse:

The association between inadequate literacy and hospital admission was strongest among patients who had been hospitalized in the year before study entry (OR 3.15; 95% CI 1.45, 6.85).3

Illiteracy is as risky, when it comes to hospital admission risk, as:

  • health failure

  • prior heart attack

  • atrial fibrillation

  • chronic kidney disease

  • COPD

  • Bipolar disorder

  • epilepsy

  • dementia

  • active cancer

So, not only is illiteracy bad for one’s readership of newsletters, but it also increases the risk of hospital admission, mortality, or other adverse outcomes, which is as severe as major brand-name illnesses.

What can we do? Well, making sure health content is accessible in terms of reading level for health organizations is one step. At Radial, we are working hard on making our content about depression (and other illnesses) accessable. However, so too is video content that is accurate and educational. We need people who can’t read to understand just as well as those who can—a tall order, but worth the effort.

1

Easton, P., Entwistle, V. A., & Williams, B. (2010). Health in the’hidden population’of people with low literacy. A systematic review of the literature. BMC public health, 10(1), 459.

2

Nancy D. Berkman, Stacey L. Sheridan, Katrina E. Donahue, et al. Low Health Literacy and Health Outcomes: An Updated Systematic Review. Ann Intern Med.2011;155:97-107.[Epub 19 July 2011]. doi:10.7326/0003-4819-155-2-201107190-00005

3

Baker, D. W., Parker, R. M., Williams, M. V., & Clark, W. S. (1998). Health literacy and the risk of hospital admission. Journal of general internal medicine, 13(12), 791-798.
